AI Changes What Chip Engineers Need To Learn

25

Shares

4

18

AI is automating routine design tasks, shifting engineering education toward architecture, specifications, verification, and the ability to evaluate results.

November 23rd, 2026 -

By: Brian Bailey

Key Takeaways:

While it remains necessary to teach fundamentals, it becomes less important to be able to use them because tools will do that.
AI can create lots of possible solutions, but it takes real skill to pick the right one. How do people productively select the best answer?
AI is adding pressure on verification methodologies to ensure slop does not enter into the flow.

Experts At The Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss how AI is changing design and verification, and how that impacts engineering school curricula, with Chuck Alpert, fellow at Cadence; Thomas Andersen, vice president of AI and ML at Synopsys; Simon Davidmann, AI and EDA researcher at University of Southampton; Nagesh Gupta, CEO of llmda.ai; Dave Kelf, CEO of Breker Verification Systems; and Kexun Zhang, co-founder and head of research at ChipAgents. What follows are excerpts of that discussion. To view part one of this discussion, click here.

Clockwise from top left: Southampton University’s Davidmann; Breker’s Kelf; Synopsys’ Andersen; ChipAgents’ Kexun; llmda’s Gupta; and Cadence’s Alpert.
SE: There is a finite amount that students can learn in the three or four years when they’re in college. What skill set do they require, and what do they stop learning in order to start taking on the new stuff that we expect them to have?
Zhang: We should still be learning the fundamentals, but a lot of the practical skills and tricks can be excluded from their textbooks and from the lectures. For example, people used to put a lot of emphasis on the ability to use logarithmic tables for big calculations, and they needed to know lots of tricks to do integrals. But now people just learn about the principles. They still need to learn the fundamentals in order to understand how these tools work, and in order to know what’s going wrong, if it goes wrong. But a lot of the very specific tricks that were intended for them to do this are no longer required. The time saved from these tricks can be used to teach higher-level abstractions.
Davidmann: It gets better than that. I remember learning how to program and how difficult the syntax was. It would take you a long time to draw a graph, for example. Now you’ve got Python, which can draw graphs. While you still need to learn the skills of programming, you don’t need to do all the development and debugging because you can generate a lot of it. You need to see the structure, and you need to define the architecture of programs and how to verify the program and test it, but you don’t do a lot of the individual coding. You won’t have to go through the practical pain of doing a lot of it because AI will do it. In the same way, when you’re doing chip architecture, you need to know about gates, but you don’t have to hand-wire up a schematic in an editor. You write some RTL, but you don’t need to know what’s down there. The education will get more abstract, as well. We need to know the fundamentals, but you’ll do less practical use of fundamentals because the tool will do it. In the research I’m doing. I started off writing lots of programs in Python at the lowest level. I don’t intend to ever do that again because I can just generate it. I set the file type I want, the structure I want, and just tell it to create the program. Then I test it. I don’t write the lines of Python anymore. I control tools to build it for me. They will learn different things, which makes them much more productive.
Alpert: Having a good curriculum is challenging. You’re teaching computer science, and you might say you have one or two weeks to do this computer science assignment, and if you use vibe coding, you can do it in an hour or two. You just have to make the assignment 10, 20 times more complex. You can build more complex systems. Teaching undergrads to do that would be fantastic.
Davidmann: At the university, one of the professors who is involved with EDA technology and chip design is setting up the curriculum for next year. They will build a RISC-V processor. We used to teach people Verilog, and the assignment would be to add a couple of Fibonacci series. There’s a company in EDA that created a RISC-V processor in 40 hours that runs Linux, completely vibe-coded. That’s the type of project they need to be doing. It’s going to be much more abstract, much higher level. Imagine a graduate who learns how to build processors. They will be in demand for a company that wants to build semiconductors. They are going to get better experience, which the industry needs, and that’s what good university courses should be able to create.
Kelf: It sounds like the expertise they’re going to have to learn is how to write good specifications that you can feed into AI.
Davidmann: It’s how to use AI efficiently, and that’s part of the challenge. The academics are challenged by this. AI is racing so fast, and the requirements that people have in industry are stressing out academics.
Alpert: When you think about verification, the whole vision of our AI system is that all you need is a good spec, and you can create all the verification collateral. You can generate the RTL. All you need is a great spec. So then the job becomes writing good specs. That’s part of it. But a big part is understanding what AI did. How do you make sure you didn’t get slop? How do you make sure you have a quality design? That’s going to be the other half of the equation.
Andersen: When something goes wrong, how do you debug it? Was it a problem in your spec? Was it a problem in the system? That is another challenge.
Davidmann: How do you know it’s got a bug in it? And then, how do you get rid of it?
Alpert: Many people in the semiconductor industry are tool jockeys. But a place-and-route person is not really doing place-and-route. They’re a tool jockey. In some sense, everybody becomes a tool jockey where they used to do it before. AI is just a tool.
Kelf: You always have verification loops. Now there’s going to be this extra verification loop up to the spec that will be used to test the output of the AI. That would be an interesting verification problem.
Zhang: The challenge is that, unlike many other tools, AI is non-deterministic. And it is more deceptive, because when it hallucinates, it sounds perfectly fine. That really adds more workload to this extra verification loop. You wouldn’t expect your traditional tools to lie to you. You wouldn’t expect your traditional tools to find a very clever way to go around your checks and your scripts and your verification suite, and give you an answer that looks perfectly fine. The reward hacking ability of AI systems is something that is not well understood, and that is a very challenging aspect of having this extra verification loop. That is also why some people — especially in domains where people did not use formal verification before, such as in a lot of software development — are now starting to realize the importance of a more rigorous way of doing verification, especially in a formal way.
Davidmann: In hardware, verification is so important because we cannot afford a failure in the chip. Software is easier to modify later. One of the key things about constrained random is that every time you run it, with a different seed, you get completely different types of tests. RTL design is going to be like that if you use Gen AI. You’re going to get a different design every time. You need repeatability to understand it. If you’re trying to find a bug, you don’t want the bug to disappear the next time you run it, and the next time it comes back because of its probabilistic nature. The specification is absolutely going to be fundamentally important, but so are verification methodologies. It’s these types of things that we need to impart on the graduates. We need to try and explain to them, educate them, about the methodologies that they need to use to get the most out of these new tools. It’s just a different type of apprenticeship. The tools are more powerful now, and they go off in different directions, so you need more understanding. It’s just a new problem for us to solve. It’s not radically different from what we did before. It’s just more abstract, maybe a bit weirder, and it’s just technology to adopt.
Gupta: There are going to be new engineering roles. AI is creating so much slop, and you’ve got to understand what it has created and when it is causing a problem. Dealing with AI slop is going to be a new career, and there is probably a significant opportunity from that perspective.
Andersen: If you look back at the history of innovations, every time you up-level something, it changes. The one thing that’s a little different with the recent AI technologies is that it is directly doing things that humans are good at, like reasoning based on seeing something, or certain data. In the past, it was more about computational things. For example, people used to be polygon pushers, or people used to write logic circuits by hand. These are not tasks that humans are naturally good at. A computational algorithm that solves wire length or chip placement will always outperform a human in the same way that a calculator outperforms me any day. But when it comes to complex reasoning tasks, that used to be the domain of the human brain. That is now being challenged. This is a different shift compared to innovations that happened before.
SE: It has been said that AI cannot do the job of a senior engineer because it doesn’t have the experience or the type of knowledge and skills required to do those tasks. So how can a junior engineer be expected to do those things, even with the help of AI?
Davidmann: You need the experience to be able to specify things, verify them, and understand them. AI can do manual things, and it can help you find issues, but it can’t really help you in the specification of what you’re trying to achieve. It doesn’t have the ability to deal with the system bits. It can only handle individual tasks. That’s why you have architects at each level. There are decisions to be made, and it’s not just grunt work. It’s intellectual work, which I’m not sure AI is close to yet.
Kelf: In fact, it does worse. You need the experience to know if the AI is putting out crap or something sensible. This is a very real problem when you’re trying to get AI to do basic tasks. It will put out something that looks pretty good initially, and then you find it’s completely hopeless. There’s something wrong with it, and a junior engineer might just rely on that, whereas a senior engineer will know it doesn’t look right. That experience is really key.
Zhang: There is this term called the verification gap, or the verification dilemma in the AI world, because AI can generate so many answers to the same question so fast. The bottleneck of getting the solution to these questions is no longer writing down the answers. It is picking one answer —  one correct and good answer — from 10,000 different answers. That is something that is different in terms of the skills required. It requires experience. It requires taste. It requires people to be able to define problems instead of just solving the problems defined by other people. Then the question becomes, ‘How do you even teach taste?’ I feel like a lot of taste comes from experience, comes from working in the industry for decades and gradually learning what’s good and what’s bad. Now that the grunt work can be done by AI, it seems that it’s important for people to accelerate that process instead of having people make mistakes — learning from the mistakes for decades — and then gradually gaining taste. Is there any way that people can be taught? Is there any way that we can cultivate this taste, which seems to be a more important ability in the AI age, now that picking what’s important to solve, picking the correct answer becomes the bottleneck? In some industries there are programs that try to teach taste, or that try to give people a fuller picture at a higher level, so that they have the ability to distinguish, but they don’t have the ability to carry out the actual work.
Gupta: That’s a very good point. The whole aspect of learning taste comes from experience. The question to ask is, what happens five years from now when you’ve lost that gap. You have all this experience that people have gained, so they understand how to do some of these things. Today, if you start off doing all of this with AI, you create a gap, and maybe AI will catch up, and it’ll understand the taste part of it. If you look at what happened in our industry 20 years ago, there was a lot of growth in other countries. We became distributed geographically. There was a lot of growth compared to the U.S. in a lot of other geographies, and in my perspective, what that has created is a void in experienced middle management in the industry. This may be a similar impact 5 years, 10 years from now. You lose that experience part of it.
Alpert: If you go back in time, EDA has always been about productivity. Designers used to be polygon pushers before place-and-route was automated. They looked at ways to organize cells to minimize the wire length. Nobody does that anymore. Now, physical design engineers are really tool jockeys. They run the PnR tools, and they are experts on how to debug them, how to read the logs, how to change the constraints. AI will take over some of that, and the engineers can move up to a higher level. Maybe the new task is how to partition blocks. The idea is that whenever EDA is able to build a new layer of abstraction, we raise people’s ability to design at a higher level. And AI is going to do exactly that. That’s a good thing. People have less grunt work, and they can do more thinking. But the problem becomes, ‘How do your junior engineers raise to that level because they don’t have the experience?’ That’s going to be a problem. As an industry we will have to figure that out, but it will happen.

Harry Foster says:

November 23, 2026 at 11:06 am

The panel raises an important question about how AI will reshape semiconductor engineering and the skills future engineers will need. I see tremendous opportunity for AI to accelerate design-space exploration, RTL development, verification, debugging, and PPA optimization, enabling engineers to explore more alternatives and tackle increasingly complex designs. But the real opportunity should extend beyond productivity to accelerating the development of engineering expertise itself. Fundamental knowledge and sound engineering judgment are built through understanding design tradeoffs, investigating failures, and confronting real implementation constraints. As AI automates more of these activities, we need to ensure that engineers, particularly those early in their careers, remain actively engaged in understanding why designs work, why they fail, and what makes one solution better than another. The goal should not simply be to automate engineering tasks (which is important), but to use AI to develop more capable engineers who can make better architectural and implementation decisions.

I feel this hits on one of the weaknesses of AI-based solutions in that they do not, or cannot, tell you why they made the decisions that they made. Without that, a junior engineer is left having to accept the solutions AI provides without the critical thinking that goes along with it. Having to debug and correct AI solutions will be tough.
